section.title: Greeting
section.sectionRationale: The letter opens unlike Paul's others: he names himself not an apostle but a prisoner, and he addresses not only Philemon but his household and the whole church that meets in his house. Every word quietly prepares the delicate appeal that will follow.
section.thesis: Paul sets aside his apostolic rank and comes as a prisoner and fellow worker, gathering Philemon, his family, and the church into one greeting of grace and peace, so that a private matter about a runaway slave is framed from the start as a family matter of the gospel.
section.frameNote: One movement in three parts: the senders, Paul and Timothy; the recipients, Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church; and the blessing of grace and peace.

units.label: Senders, recipients, and blessing
units.note: a prisoner writes to a household and a church

verses.text: Paul, a {{desmios|prisoner}} of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved {{synergos|fellow worker}},
to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets at your house:
{{charis|Grace}} and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

desmios.gloss: A prisoner, one held in chains or bonds. In most of his letters Paul opens by claiming his title as an apostle; here he opens as a prisoner of Christ Jesus. He appeals from weakness and love rather than rank, and his chains, mentioned again and again, set the humble tone of the whole letter.

synergos.gloss: A fellow worker or co-laborer. Paul greets Philemon not as a subordinate to be commanded but as a partner in the work of the gospel. The word lays the relational groundwork for the request Paul is about to make, appealing to a shared labor and love.

charis.gloss: Grace, undeserved favor and kindness. It is Paul's customary greeting, but it is freighted here: the entire letter is a plea that the grace Philemon has received from God would now flow out of him toward a returning slave who has no claim on him.

basic.context: Paul is in prison, and from his cell he writes a short, personal letter to Philemon, a well-off Christian in the town of Colossae whose home hosts a church. Paul had led Philemon to faith. The whole letter concerns Onesimus, Philemon's slave, who ran away, met Paul in prison, and became a Christian. These first three verses are simply the greeting: Paul names the senders, the people he is writing to, and prays grace and peace over them all.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real letter to a real man about a real and awkward situation. Paul could have pulled rank as an apostle and given orders. Instead he calls himself a prisoner and a fellow worker, and he lets the whole church listen in. The way he opens teaches us how the gospel reshapes even how we ask people for hard things.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul calls himself a desmios, a prisoner in chains, not an apostle. He calls Philemon a synergos, a fellow worker, a partner rather than an underling. And he opens with charis, grace, the same grace he will soon ask Philemon to show. The words are gentle on purpose.
basic.typology: There is no formal type here, but the shape of things points ahead. A greeting of grace and peace flows from the Father and the Lord Jesus, the very grace that will be asked to travel from a master to a slave, picturing how God's grace to us is meant to move through us to others.
basic.christ: Everything is anchored in Christ Jesus. Paul is His prisoner, the grace and peace come through Him, and the reconciliation the letter seeks is only possible because of Him. Christ is named in every verse of this greeting, the ground on which enemies can become family.
basic.god: God is Father, the source of grace and peace, and the One who binds strangers into one household. He is generous, giving grace freely, and He is the One from whom all true peace between people flows.
basic.crossReferences: Colossians 4:9 calls Onesimus one of the Colossians, tying this letter to that church. Ephesians 3:1 and 4:1 show Paul again calling himself a prisoner of Christ. Numbers 6 lies behind the ancient blessing of grace and peace.
basic.oneStory: The gospel gathers people into one family under one Father. This small greeting, sent from a prison to a house church, is a snapshot of the whole Bible's aim: grace from God creating a people at peace with Him and with one another.

context.literary:
Verses 1 to 3 are an address formula, and the grammar shows it. There is no main verb in the three verses. The senders stand in the nominative, the recipients in the dative, and the greeting hangs off both, which is exactly how an ordinary Greek letter began. Paul does something with that frame that the other letters only hint at. He does not use the title of authority he wears in Romans 1:1, 1 Corinthians 1:1 or Colossians 1:1, where he is an apostle. He is not even the 'servant' of Philippians 1:1. He is simply a prisoner, and the only word of rank in the whole opening is the word that belongs to Christ.

The address is built in rings. Two senders, Paul and Timothy, face four named recipients and a gathered church. The first sender is a prisoner and the first recipient is a fellow worker. The list moves from the man to the woman to the man to the assembly, widening as it goes, until a private matter between two men has become a matter before a congregation. The closing line of the letter is built the same way. Everywhere else in the letter 'you' is singular, but the footnote to verse 2 notes that the pronouns are plural in verses 3, 22 and 25. The greeting, the promise of a visit, and the final blessing are spoken to everyone, and the appeal in between is spoken to one man in the hearing of all.

Grace opens the letter in verse 3 and closes it in verse 25, 'The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.' The whole letter sits inside that inclusio, so the request about Onesimus is asked and answered within grace.

The titles are worth listing. Paul is a prisoner; Timothy is a brother; Philemon is beloved and a fellow worker; Apphia is a sister; Archippus is a fellow soldier. These are family and field words, and none of them is a word of command. Even the list of persons is part of the argument, because Paul is quietly arranging the room in which Onesimus will be received.
context.historical:
Colossae lay in the Lycus valley in the Roman province of Asia, close to Laodicea and Hierapolis, the two neighbours Paul names in Colossians 4:13. Philemon belongs to that town. Colossians 4:9 describes Onesimus as 'one of you,' which ties the slave to the same community, and the two letters appear to have travelled together, since Tychicus carries Colossians and Onesimus goes with him, Colossians 4:7-9. The names of the greeters in Philemon 23 and 24 are almost the names in Colossians 4:10-14, which fixes the two letters to one moment of Paul's custody.

Paul did not found the church at Colossae. Epaphras did, Colossians 1:7 and 4:12, and Paul speaks of those 'who have not met me face to face,' Colossians 2:1. That makes Philemon's debt in verse 19 a notable one. Philemon came to faith under Paul's ministry somewhere other than Colossae, quite possibly during the long Ephesian years described in Acts 19:10, when 'everyone who lived in the province of Asia' heard the word. He then went home and opened his house.

Early churches met in homes of the better off: Prisca and Aquila, Romans 16:5 and 1 Corinthians 16:19, and Nympha at Laodicea, Colossians 4:15. A house of that size held more than a family. It held slaves, freedpeople, clients and guests, and in Roman law the head of the household held power over all of them. A letter addressed 'to the church that meets at your house' therefore addressed a room that already included the man's own dependants.

The place of Paul's imprisonment is not stated in the letter. Rome fits Acts 28:16-31, where Paul lived under guard and received visitors for two years. Ephesus and Caesarea have also been proposed, and the question is taken up below.
context.canonical:
The words 'grace and peace' open every letter Paul wrote that bears his name in the New Testament, and the form in verse 3 is the one in Romans 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:3 and Philippians 1:2. Behind it many readers hear the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26, where the LORD is asked to be gracious and to give peace. The words that Aaron's sons spoke over Israel are spoken here over a house church, with the Lord Jesus placed beside the Father as their source.

The self-description 'a prisoner of Christ Jesus' returns in Ephesians 3:1, 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles,' in Ephesians 4:1, and in 2 Timothy 1:8, 'His prisoner.' Paul reads his chains as a post Christ has given him, and Ephesians 6:20 calls him 'an ambassador in chains.' Hebrews 13:3 later tells the whole church to remember prisoners 'as if you were bound with them,' and in Colossians 4:18 Paul closes with 'Remember my chains,' which is the same call.

The little company in verses 23 and 24 has a later history. Mark is the man whom Paul will once again find 'useful to me in the ministry,' 2 Timothy 4:11, a word that links back to Onesimus in verse 11. Luke is the physician and, by tradition, the author of Luke and Acts. Demas is the sad name, for 2 Timothy 4:10 says that he 'in his love of this world, has deserted me.' The list shows that a person named in the greeting of Scripture is not thereby secured, and that restoration, like Mark's, is worth waiting for.

The house church motif carries from Acts 2:46, 'from house to house,' to Romans 16:5 and Colossians 4:15, and the household of God is a major theme of Ephesians 2:19 and Hebrews 3:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant Philemon to hear, before he heard the request, how the request would be made. A letter that began with 'Paul, an apostle' would have opened a chain of command. A letter that begins with a prisoner, a co-sender and a gathered church opens a family conversation. Every title in verses 1 and 2 is chosen to make the coming appeal a matter of love between brothers and not an order from an official, and Paul says as much in verses 8 and 9.

He also meant the church to be a party. By naming Apphia, Archippus and the assembly in the house, Paul makes Philemon's answer a public one. This is not a threat. Paul is giving Philemon a community to act within, so that he will not be left to decide in private against the pressures of his own household and his standing. A man who has to explain himself before the church is also a man who is supported by the church.

Third, Paul meant Philemon to know where he stood. He is a prisoner of Christ, not of Caesar, so the one who has the chains also has the authority, and that authority is Christ's. By writing 'grace' first, he tells Philemon that the question is how Christ's grace will pass through him, not how the law will treat Onesimus.

It is a small letter, but the opening is already a theology of how Christians ask each other for hard things.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The opening records a prisoner writing from custody to a household and a congregation. It does not command anything. We are not told that leaders must lay down their titles, that every letter must name a whole assembly, or that churches must meet in homes. Those are details of one first century situation.

What the passage does teach by example is how to begin. Paul begins with relationship, with names, with the language of family, and with the word grace. A reader today can imitate this without copying it. A pastor, a parent or a manager who has to ask for something costly can choose to lead with kinship and gratitude before authority, and can bring in witnesses who love both parties.

Care is needed with the 'fellow soldier' and 'fellow worker' labels. They describe the shared labour of the gospel, not a licence to treat the church as a military unit or a company. And the house setting should not be turned into a rule that only homes are proper. The text describes what the believers at Colossae did, and says nothing against other places.

debates.question: Why does Paul call himself a prisoner rather than an apostle here?

views.label: A deliberate appeal to love, not authority
views.case: Paul chooses not to pull rank because he wants Philemon's obedience to be free and glad, not compelled. Naming himself a prisoner evokes sympathy and sets the humble tone the whole letter needs.

views.label: A simple reflection of his circumstances
views.case: Paul is in fact in chains, and the title honestly names where he writes from and why his ministry now takes this personal, pleading form.

debates.bearing: Either way, the self-description shapes the letter: Paul comes low, as a prisoner and partner, so that reconciliation will be won by love rather than forced by rank.

debates.question: Where was Paul when he wrote Philemon?

views.label: Rome
views.case: This is the traditional view. Acts 28:16-31 shows Paul under guard for two years and still teaching, and the later years in Rome supply the time for Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Luke and Demas to gather around him. The distance from Rome to Colossae is long, but a fugitive slave would naturally head for a great city where he could disappear, and Paul would have found him there.

views.label: Ephesus
views.case: Ephesus is close to Colossae, so a runaway could reach Paul quickly and a visit in verse 22 could happen soon. Paul speaks of 'more imprisonments,' 2 Corinthians 11:23, and Acts 19:10 describes a long Ephesian ministry. The letter itself does not name any imprisonment at Ephesus, though, and Acts does not record one.

views.label: Caesarea
views.case: Paul was held in Caesarea for two years, Acts 24:27, and some have placed the letter there. It is the least often held view because the distance is great and the hope of lodging in verse 22 fits less easily.

debates.bearing: The letter's message does not depend on the answer. Under every view Paul writes as a prisoner who hopes to be restored to them and cannot visit. What the choice changes is how long Onesimus had been away and how long the letter and its bearer took to travel.

study.originalLanguages:
Five small points of Greek carry more of Paul's meaning than the English shows, and the first of them is the grammar of the title Paul chose.

First, 'a prisoner of Christ Jesus' is a genitive, and genitives can point two ways. Paul may be a prisoner for Christ's cause, or a prisoner who belongs to Christ. Ephesians 3:1 adds 'for the sake of you Gentiles,' which fixes the first sense there, but the plain genitive here lets both stand. The phrase says that the chains have an owner, and the owner is not Rome.

Second, the family and love words run through the letter. 'Beloved' in verse 1 is agapetos, from the same root as agape, 'love,' and that root returns in verses 5, 7, 9 and 16. The opening word of address and the letter's repeated word for the ground of the appeal are the same. Likewise adelphos, 'brother,' and its feminine adelphe, 'sister,' in verse 2, is the word Paul will apply to Onesimus in verse 16. By using it for Timothy and Apphia he trains the ear.

Third, 'fellow soldier,' systratiotes, is a word with a camp in it. Paul uses it again of Epaphroditus in Philippians 2:25, who was 'my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier.' Archippus is given that dignity, and the title honours a man who is later told to finish a task, Colossians 4:17.

Fourth, 'peace' in verse 3 translates eirene, which in the Septuagint regularly renders the Hebrew shalom, a word for wholeness and well being that reaches well beyond the absence of conflict. 'Grace and peace' sets the Greek greeting stem beside the Hebrew greeting. Christian use took a common wish and filled it with the gospel, as Romans 5:1 does when it says that those justified 'have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.'

Fifth, verse 3 says 'from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,' and the single preposition 'from' governs both. The Father and the Lord Jesus are the one source of grace. And in a household letter the title 'Lord,' kyrios, is no small word. It was the common word for a master over slaves, so that Colossians 4:1 can tell masters that they 'also have a Master in heaven.' Philemon is greeted by a letter that uses his own title for Jesus.

typology.type: The priestly blessing and the greeting of grace and peace, Numbers 6:24-26
typology.fulfillment: Aaron's sons were to put the LORD's name on Israel by asking that He be gracious and give peace. Paul's 'grace and peace' is not a quotation of the blessing, so the link is an echo and not a proof. The echo is worth hearing because of what Christ adds: peace now has a person for its source, Ephesians 2:14, 'He Himself is our peace.' The blessing in Numbers fell on one nation at one sanctuary; this one reaches a house church in Phrygia and names the Lord Jesus beside the Father. The type falls short in that the old blessing came through a priest who could not guarantee its content, while the new comes from the One who made peace by the blood of His cross, Colossians 1:20.

typology.type: The house church and the household of God, Ephesians 2:19
typology.fulfillment: The tabernacle and temple were God's house in Israel, a place where His people met Him under rules of distance. The assembly in Philemon's living room is a small picture of what Ephesians 2:19 calls God's household and of what Hebrews 3:6 means by 'we are His house.' The correspondence is real but partial, because the church is not a building and no room is holier than another. The escalation lies in Christ, who is 'faithful as the Son over God's house,' Hebrews 3:6, and who makes slaves and masters members of one household together.

typology.type: The prisoner who belongs to another, Philemon 1
typology.fulfillment: Paul is bound, yet writes as one who is held by Christ and not by Caesar. This is a pattern more than a type, and it must not be pressed. It echoes the way Scripture again and again shows God's servants carrying His purposes in confinement, as with Joseph, and it points past them to the Servant who 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7. Paul's chains are real, and he asks Philemon to remember them, Colossians 4:18. They are not saving chains. Only Christ's cross is, and that is where the pattern stops.

study.christ:
Christ is named in each of the three verses, and the way He is named is the first lesson. Paul is 'a prisoner of Christ Jesus,' not Caesar's, so the one who holds his life is the Lord. He begins with Christ because everything he will say about slaves and brothers rests on who Christ is and what He has done.

Christ is placed with the Father as the source of grace and peace. A devout Jew, which Paul was, would not casually write 'grace and peace from God and from a man.' By putting 'God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' under one preposition, Paul assumes the deity of Jesus without arguing it. The grace that will cost Philemon something is not Paul's gift to give; it flows from Christ, who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. That is why the letter can ask for grace without pleading for it.

Christ is the one who makes the peace that the whole letter wants. Ephesians 2:14-16 says that He 'has made the two one,' tearing down 'the dividing wall of hostility,' and Colossians 1:20 says that He made peace 'through the blood of His cross.' Those verses speak of Jew and Gentile, and Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11 carry the same logic to 'slave or free.' The peace Paul wishes on this house is not a social ceasefire; it is the peace that comes from the cross.

Christ is also the Master whose own mastery changes every other. 'He who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord's freedman,' 1 Corinthians 7:22. Masters are told that they 'also have a Master in heaven,' Colossians 4:1. When the greeting calls Jesus 'Lord' it places Philemon, who is a lord in his house, beneath the Lord who rules his house.

And Christ is the brother who makes the family language true. 'Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers,' Hebrews 2:11. The titles Paul hands out in verses 1 and 2 are not courtesies. They rest on the fact that the Son has become family with those He saves, and that Philemon and Onesimus have the same Elder Brother.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Philemon is not a letter in code about Jesus, and Paul is not Christ. What the greeting supplies is the ground and the pattern: who gives grace, who makes peace, and who owns the chains.
study.god:
The first thing the greeting shows about God is that He is Father. 'God our Father' is a family word, and the plural 'our' pulls Paul, Timothy, Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church into one relation. Ephesians 3:14-15 says that 'every family in heaven and on earth derives its name' from the Father. If one Father names every family, the claim of verse 16, that a slave can be a brother, is not a stretch of sentiment; it is a consequence of who God is.

God is the source. Grace and peace come 'from God,' which means they are gifts and not achievements. Paul's own work in prayer, his writing and his chains are all instruments. This is why he can thank God, not Philemon, in verse 4, and why in verse 25 he can end with grace as a wish for the whole house. The order matters too: grace comes first, and peace follows, as in Romans 5:1-2, where peace with God comes through justification and access 'into this grace in which we stand.'

God is impartial. Colossians 3:25 and Ephesians 6:9 say there is 'no favoritism' with Him, and both sit within household instructions to masters and slaves, the same ones Colossians sends to this very town. In Philemon's household the same Master rules slave and owner. The greeting is addressed to a man who will be expected to live under that impartial rule.

God is near and gathers. He meets with a church in a home, not only in a temple, and the setting says something about how He is known: among a few believers around a table, and through ordinary hospitality. He is not tied to a building, to a class, or to the free.

God also works through the confinement of His servants. Paul does not complain of his chains; he turns them into a ministry, as in 2 Timothy 2:9, 'the word of God cannot be chained.' The reader is left to hold together God's sovereign care and Paul's real suffering without explaining either away.

For worship, the lesson is to ask how we greet each other. If God is Father and gives grace first, then our first words to a brother or sister who owes us something should come out of that grace, and the request, whatever it is, should follow.

crossReferences.note: Tychicus and Onesimus travel together to Colossae with Paul's letter to the church. Paul calls Onesimus 'our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you,' words that anticipate the verdict he asks from Philemon in verse 16. The two letters were written to be read in the same house church, so the greeting here and the greeting in Colossians belong together.

'See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord.' Archippus, whom Philemon 2 calls a fellow soldier, is addressed by name in the Colossian letter. The text does not say what his ministry was, and readers should not invent it. The link shows that the church that heard Philemon also heard a charge to Archippus, and that the pressure on this household was public.

The same five names, Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphras, Luke and Demas, appear here with Paul and in Philemon 23 and 24, though in a different order. The overlap shows that both letters were written in the same season. Epaphras, who is 'one of you,' wrestles in prayer for the Colossians, which explains why the greeting from him is warm.

'The prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles.' Paul's self-title in Philemon 1 has the same shape, and Ephesians adds the purpose: he is bound because of the gospel for others. It helps readers see that 'prisoner of Christ' is both a fact about Rome and a claim about whose he is.

Paul calls Epaphroditus 'my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier,' the three titles that this letter spreads across Timothy, Philemon and Archippus. It shows that Paul's vocabulary of kinship and campaign is a habit of his, and that it was used to honour workers, not to command them.

The priestly blessing asks that the LORD 'be gracious to you' and 'give you peace.' Paul's 'grace and peace' is not a quotation, but the pairing is the same, and the blessing that once rested on a nation is spoken over one house church, with the Lord Jesus named beside the Father.

'Greet also the church that meets at their house,' Paul writes of Prisca and Aquila. House churches were the ordinary form of congregation in the first generation, and the prominence of homeowners like Philemon explains why this private letter could be read publicly with no strain.

Demas, who greets Philemon with Paul, later 'in his love of this world, has deserted me,' while Mark is called 'useful to me in the ministry.' The two names in the same short list show that the greeting records a moment, not a guarantee, and that Mark's restoration lies ahead.

'He Himself is our peace.' Paul says that Christ tore down the wall of hostility and made one new people. It supplies the content of the 'peace' in Philemon 3: not a mood, but a reconciliation that makes strangers family, which is what the letter will ask Philemon to practise.

'Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.' The family titles that Paul distributes in the greeting rest on this: the Son who sanctifies shares a family with those He sanctifies, and so a master and a slave in Christ share the one Elder Brother.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible opens with a household. God makes human beings in His image, male and female, to live with Him and under Him, Genesis 1:26-27, and the first scene of trouble is a hiding, 'Where are you?' Genesis 3:9. Within a chapter or two the broken household produces a brother who asks, 'Am I my brother's keeper?' Genesis 4:9. Sin does not only separate people from God; it splits families and turns them into rivals and owners. Every later chapter of the story is, in part, a search for how the family can be gathered again.

God answers that search with a promise to one man: 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3. The families are plural, and the blessing is meant for them. Israel's life under the law, with its sabbaths, jubilees and its care for strangers, was a first sketch of a household under God. It was only a sketch, because Israel itself was a house that could free its slaves and then take them back, Jeremiah 34:8-17, and the prophets looked for a day when the nations would stream to God's house and learn peace, Isaiah 2:2-4.

The greeting of Philemon is a small piece of that fulfilment. A prisoner in a Roman cell, a well off householder in Phrygia, a woman, a soldier, and a church in a living room are called by one Father and one Lord. They share 'grace and peace.' The ancient blessing has gone out from a priest's lips to ordinary homes, and the family promised to Abraham is meeting around tables, with strangers and foreigners 'fellow citizens with the saints,' Ephesians 2:19.

The story is not finished in this letter, and the letter itself knows it. The relationships it names are strained by the situation with Onesimus, and the whole appeal is the work of making a fractured family whole in one place. That is what the gospel does in the middle of the story: it puts the new household into the old world while the old world is still structured by owners and slaves, and lets the new household press on the old.

The ending is a household too. A great multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' stands before the throne, Revelation 7:9-10, and God's dwelling is 'with man,' Revelation 21:3. 'No longer will there be any curse,' and 'His servants will worship Him,' Revelation 22:3. The grace and peace that begin Philemon are the first small taste of that gathered, peaceful, worshipping family.

sermon.title: Terms of Endearment
sermon.why: The opening message of Begg's series A Study in Philemon covers Philemon 1:1-7, working through the greeting and Paul's warm terms of endearment, and showing how the gospel shapes the way Paul approaches Philemon. A clear, orthodox handling of this movement's opening.

quiz.q: Why does Paul call himself a prisoner rather than an apostle at the start of this letter?

options.text: He appeals from love and humility rather than pulling rank, to win a free and glad response.
options.note: Paul deliberately comes low, as a prisoner and fellow worker, so reconciliation is won by love, not command.

options.text: He was simply stating that he was in prison at the time.
options.note: True, he was in chains, but the choice of title is deliberate and shapes the whole appeal.

options.text: He had lost his authority as an apostle.
options.note: Paul still holds apostolic authority; he chooses not to lean on it here.

options.text: He wanted Philemon to feel sorry for him and obey out of guilt.
options.note: Paul seeks a willing response of love, not a guilt-driven one.

quiz.q: Who does Paul address in the greeting?

options.text: Philemon, along with Apphia, Archippus, and the whole church that meets in his house.
options.note: Paul widens a private matter to include the household and church as loving witnesses.

options.text: Only Philemon, since the matter was private.
options.note: Philemon is the main recipient, but Paul deliberately draws in his family and church too.
This is a letter to a Christian household and church, not to civic authorities.
The letter is about Onesimus but addressed to Philemon and his church.

quiz.q: What does Paul pray over Philemon and the church?

options.text: Grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
options.note: The very grace Paul prays down is the grace he will soon ask Philemon to show Onesimus.

options.text: God's blessing and keeping over them all.
options.note: A true summary of his heart, but Paul's specific words are grace and peace.

options.text: Health and prosperity in this life.
options.note: Paul's blessing is spiritual grace and peace, not material wellbeing.

options.text: Nothing; he moves straight to his demands.
options.note: Paul opens with a warm blessing before any request.

quiz.q: How is Christ present in these three opening verses?

options.text: He is named in every verse, the ground of Paul's imprisonment, the source of grace and peace, and the basis of reconciliation.
options.note: The whole appeal rests on the peace Christ has already secured.

options.text: He is mentioned once, in passing.
options.note: In fact Christ Jesus is named throughout the greeting, not just once.

options.text: He is not mentioned until later in the letter.
options.note: Christ is central from the very first verse.

options.text: He appears only as an example to imitate.
options.note: Christ is far more than an example here; He is the ground of the whole appeal.

questions: Paul could have given orders but chose to appeal as a fellow worker. When you need something hard from someone, do you tend to pull rank or to appeal in love, and what would change if you followed Paul's way?
Paul opens with grace and peace before raising anything difficult. How might beginning your hardest conversations with genuine blessing reshape them?
The greeting draws a whole church into one man's private matter. Who are the people God has placed around you to help carry your relationships toward reconciliation?
Paul calls himself a prisoner of Christ, not merely a prisoner of Rome. How does seeing your own limits and hardships as being in Christ's hands change the way you carry them?
The grace Paul prays down is the grace he will soon ask Philemon to give away. Where is God asking you to pass on to others the grace you have received from Him?

translationNotes.note: The words you and your are singular throughout this letter, addressed to Philemon personally, except in verses 3, 22, and 25, where they widen to the whole gathered church.
The church that meets at your house reflects the early practice of congregations gathering in believers' homes; Philemon's home was large enough to host such a gathering.
